title: Linux Fundamentals III: packages, networking and automation
description: Install software, understand ports and connections from the terminal, and take your first steps with bash and cron.

1.title: Packages: install and update
1.body:
## The package manager is your app store

| Family | Install | Search | Update everything |
|---|---|---|---|
| Debian/Ubuntu | `apt install nmap` | `apt search nmap` | `apt update && apt upgrade` |
| Fedora/RHEL | `dnf install nmap` | `dnf search nmap` | `dnf upgrade` |
| Arch | `pacman -S nmap` | `pacman -Ss nmap` | `pacman -Syu` |
| Alpine | `apk add nmap` | `apk search nmap` | `apk upgrade` |

Golden rule: ALWAYS install from official (signed) repositories. A `.deb` or
`.rpm` downloaded from some random website is the classic way to install a backdoor.

```bash
apt update          # refresh the indexes (ALWAYS first)
apt upgrade         # apply updates
apt remove nmap     # uninstall
dpkg -l | grep nmap # is it installed? (package level)
```

Keeping the system up to date is the most cost-effective mitigation there is — both for
your machines and for the ones you're going to audit (old versions = known CVEs?).

linux-fundamentos-3-t01-q01.prompt: On Debian/Ubuntu, which command DOWNLOADS and installs a package (e.g. nmap) in a single step?
linux-fundamentos-3-t01-q01.hint: Like apt-get install… but without the '-get'.

linux-fundamentos-3-t01-q02.prompt: Which distribution family uses dnf/rpm instead of apt/deb?
linux-fundamentos-3-t01-q02.hint: The one with the red hat.

2.title: Networking from the terminal
2.body:
## Which ports do I have open, and who is using them?

```bash
ip a                    # my interfaces and IPs (successor of ifconfig)
ss -tulpn               # listening TCP/UDP ports + process
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8       # is there a way out to the internet?
traceroute 8.8.8.8      # the path of hops
```

`ss -tulpn` is one of the first things you'll run on a compromised machine:
**a service listening only on 127.0.0.1** = a classic possible lateral move
(bound to localhost, reachable through an SSH tunnel). Listening on `0.0.0.0` = all
interfaces, potentially exposed.

## curl: your HTTP Swiss Army knife

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/           # simple GET
curl -I http://ejemplo.com/           # headers only
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"user":"ana"}' http://api.local/login
curl -o archivo.zip URL               # download
```

You already know curl from the recon lab — here it becomes an everyday tool. In the
Networking module we'll dig deeper into TCP/IP, DNS and Wireshark captures.

linux-fundamentos-3-t02-q01.prompt: Which command lists LISTENING ports along with their process (the successor of netstat)?
linux-fundamentos-3-t02-q01.hint: Two s's; the -l option means listening, -p means process.

linux-fundamentos-3-t02-q02.prompt: Which tool downloads/shows a URL and sends POST requests with JSON (you'll use it with every API)?

linux-fundamentos-3-t02-q03.prompt: Is a port in LISTEN state on 127.0.0.1:8080 reachable from another machine on the network?
linux-fundamentos-3-t02-q03.hint: Think about the interface it's listening on.

options.a: Yes, every LISTEN port is public
options.b: No: only from the machine itself (loopback)
options.c: Only if the firewall is open

3.title: Your first script and scheduled tasks
3.body:
## Scripts: saving commands for the future

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# enumerar.sh — first reconnaissance round on a machine
set -e
echo "== identidad =="; whoami; id
echo "== suid ==";    find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
echo "== puertos =="; ss -tulpn | head -15
```

Save it as `enumerar.sh`, give it execute permission and run it:

```bash
chmod +x enumerar.sh
./enumerar.sh            # or bash enumerar.sh
```

Variables (`DESTINO=10.10.10.5`, then `$DESTINO`), loops (`for puerto in 22 80 443`) and
conditionals turn commands into your own tools. In the scripting module of the
Jr Pentester path you'll build a port scanner in bash and Python.

## Cron: time runs code too

```bash
crontab -e               # edit YOUR tasks
cat /etc/crontab         # system tasks
ls -la /etc/cron.d/      # per-package tasks
```

Format: `minuto hora día-del-mes mes día-de-la-semana comando` (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, command).

```
30 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
```

For an attacker, a root cron job that runs a writable script is immediate
escalation; for a defender, reviewing cron is part of hunting for persistence.
Linux module complete — Windows and Active Directory are waiting for you.
